title: ROLEX OYSTERQUARTZ DATEJUST 17000 BLACK DIAL FULL SET
description: If you close your eyes and picture a 1970s steel sports watch with an integrated bracelet, the first models that come to mind are probably the Audemars Piguet Royal Oak and the Patek Philippe Nautilus, and understandably so. However, Rolex also made a watch that fits this exact description, and in my opinion, it’s one of the coolest designs the brand has ever produced. The Oysterquartz Datejust, introduced in 1977, was Rolex’s answer to the quartz crisis, joining the efforts of other top Swiss watchmakers of the era. This bold yet sleek integrated-bracelet watch stood apart from the brand’s other offerings, with an angular silhouette of sharp bevels and chamfers. Avant-garde by Rolex standards, it wasn’t an instant hit. Although it remained in the Rolex line-up until around 2001, production numbers were significantly lower than those of its automatic counterparts, with only around 1,000 leaving the factory each year. Decades later, collectors and enthusiasts have finally begun to recognise this hidden gem, and Oysterquartz models are now receiving the attention they deserve. Its Genta-esque integrated bracelet design remains a true outlier in Rolex’s history. The Ref. 17000 here dates from 1987 and has a gorgeous black dial. Now nearly 40 years old, it was serviced by Rolex in 2024 and has remained unworn since. The lightly polished case remains strong, and the bracelet shows no wear. The dial is flawless, with tritium lume plots that have aged to a light creamy hue. The watch comes with its original box, warranty papers, tag and Rolex NFC service card. A wonderful example of one of the coolest Rolexes of the 1980s.

title: ROLEX DATEJUST 1601/8 CHAMPAGNE DIAL
description: The Rolex Datejust, introduced in 1945 as the world’s first self-winding wristwatch with a date window, has been a cornerstone of the Rolex line-up for more than 80 years. Nowadays, however, many see the Datejust as an “entry-level” Rolex: a more accessible option for those dipping their toes into vintage collecting, or the “first watch to ask for” at your local AD to get on the list an Oysterflex Daytona. Not all Datejusts were created equal, though. While most 1601s were made in stainless steel or steel and gold, typically on Jubilee bracelets, a select few were crafted entirely in precious metal, such as the 18k yellow gold example we have here. The 1601/8 was also offered on the President bracelet, more commonly associated with the Day-Date. This watch has survived in remarkable condition after nearly 60 years. The sunburst champagne dial is near perfect, with all the tritium lume plots intact and aged to a beautiful creamy hue. The case has been polished but remains strong. The original President bracelet shows minor stretch and is one link short, fitting wrists of up to 19cm. The movement came to us in excellent health, running at +1 s/d, with 290° amplitude and a 0.1 ms beat error. Early four-digit gold Datejusts on bracelet are extremely hard to find, even more so than their Day-Date counterparts, especially in good condition. They wear beautifully on the wrist, and that warm shade of gold is to die for.

title: ROLEX SUBMARINER DATE 1680 MK2
description: Rolex released the Ref. 1680 in 1967 as the original “Date Sub”, more than a decade after the Submariner’s debut. It had a distinctly different case design and a unique “Top Hat” crystal with the iconic Cyclops magnifier. Examples from the first decade of production are affectionately known as “Red Subs”, thanks to the distinctive red lettering on their dials. Over time, the Red Sub has become one of the most sought-after vintage Rolex models: a grail for many collectors, with a price tag to match. By comparison, 1680s with white text are perhaps some of the most underappreciated vintage Rolexes. Produced between 1976 and 1979, they came with three dial variants. The present example from 1977 has a Mk2 dial and is in superb condition. The tritium lume on the markers and hands has aged to a gentle, creamy hue, and the bezel insert has faded heavily to a “ghost” colour. The case has been polished in the past. The movement has been freshly serviced and is running at +3 s/d, with 286° amplitude and a 0.1 ms beat error. An honest example of a Rolex icon.

title: ROLEX GMT MASTER 1675 FUCHSIA MK1 TROPICAL DIAL
description: The GMT-Master 1675 is easily one of the most exciting references in vintage Rolex collecting, and my personal favourite. Not only did it go through numerous variations during more than 20 years of production, but thanks to its colourful bezels and the different lacquers, paints and lume used, each example has developed a truly individual character over the decades, often beautiful in very different ways. This 1967 example has one of the most attractive configurations among matte-dial 1675s: a Mk1 dial paired with a “fuchsia” insert, named for its dark pink tone rather than the usual red. This anomaly appears only within a very narrow serial range, often overlapping with early Long E dials. The watch has been preserved in wonderful condition, with a very strong case (just look at the crown guards). The early Mk1 dial has taken on a tropical brown hue, which is especially obvious next to a matte black example, and the tritium lume has aged to an even, creamy hue. The original C&I rivet bracelet has no stretch. The movement was serviced within the last year and is running perfectly at −1 s/d, with 285° amplitude and a 0.2 ms beat error. A fuchsia 1675 has long been a grail for many watch nerds. Unfortunately, many on the market are incorrect or have faded “Pepsi” inserts rather than true fuchsias. This is easily one of the best examples I’ve ever handled.

title: ROLEX GMT-MASTER 1675 PCG SERVICE DIAL
description: The GMT-Master 1675 is easily one of the most exciting references in vintage Rolex collecting, and my personal favourite. Not only did it go through numerous variations during more than 20 years of production, but thanks to its colourful bezels and the different lacquers, paints and lume used, each example has developed a truly individual character over the decades, often beautiful in very different ways. This 1964 example shows what can become of a 1675 after six decades, through a combination of natural ageing and human (Rolex) intervention. If you asked me to pick just one vintage Rolex, I’d most likely choose a pointed-crown-guard (PCG) 1675 with a glossy gilt dial, which is exactly the configuration this watch left the factory with. The original PCG case has been amazingly well preserved, especially the crown guards. During a Rolex service more than a decade ago, however, the dial, hands, bracelet and insert were all replaced, bringing the watch back to full factory functionality. The lugs have been polished too. Curiously, the watch has clearly been worn very little, if at all, since then. The bracelet is in as-new condition, and there are barely any marks on the case. The movement is also running perfectly at +5 s/d, with 275° amplitude and a 0.1 ms beat error. An all-original example could easily cost twice as much, if not more. This watch, by contrast, offers a great way to enjoy a PCG 1675 every day (with functional lume, no less) for a price similar to a 16710, or a few thousand pounds less than a modern BLRO.

title: ROLEX EXPLORER II 16570 'BLACK TRITIUM DIAL'
description: For many years, the Rolex Explorer II was an underappreciated gem in the world of vintage Rolex collecting. That has changed in recent times, with early references such as the 1655 “Steve McQueen” and the 16550 now commanding serious attention from collectors, along with ever-increasing price tags. The Ref. 16550 was produced for just four years before being succeeded by the 16570 in 1989. The 16570 then enjoyed a substantial 22-year production run before being replaced by its larger 42mm successor. Over this long lifespan, Rolex introduced numerous subtle changes to the dial, case and bracelet. The watch offered here came from the early days of 16570s' production . The tritium lume on the markers has aged to a deep, creamy hue, while the hands are slightly lighter, a common trait for this reference. The case is exceptionally strong and has probably been polished no more than once in its lifetime. The 78360 bracelet has just been serviced by Michael Young and is in as-new condition. That warmth in the lume makes all the difference on a black-dial Explorer II, and this is an exceptionally beautiful watch on the wrist.

title: ROLEX GMT-MASTER 1675 TYPE C GILT DIAL
description: The GMT-Master 1675 is easily one of the most exciting references in vintage Rolex collecting, and my personal favourite. Not only did it go through numerous variations during more than 20 years of production, but thanks to its colourful bezels and the different lacquers, paints and lume used, each example has developed a truly individual character over the decades, often beautiful in very different ways. The present example dates from late 1966 and has a Type C “narrow Swiss” dial. The galvanic gilt dial is flawless, with gorgeous tritium markers and a perfect mirror finish. The hour, minute, seconds and GMT hands all have matching lume, which glows brightly under UV before fading away. The case has only been very lightly polished, and the insert has aged to an attractive light blue and copper. The original 6251H bracelet with 1969 clasp has only very mild stretch. The watch is running smoothly at +3 s/d, with 267° amplitude and a 0.2 ms beat error. There’s just nothing quite like a gilt 1675.

title: ROLEX SUBMARINER 14060M TWO LINER FULL SET
description: The Rolex Submariner 14060 was introduced in 1990, replacing the 5513, which had enjoyed a glorious 28-year production run. Although it looked similar to the white gold surround (WGS) 5513, the 14060 brought several key updates, including a sapphire crystal, the calibre 3000 movement and a unidirectional bezel. These significantly improved its functionality and robustness, while retaining the clean, symmetrical no-date look of the iconic Submariner. Over its production life, the 14060 went through several notable changes: from tritium to LumiNova dials and later, in 1999, to the 14060M (“modified”), which introduced a Super-LumiNova dial and the modern calibre 3130. This 2004 14060M has a two-line Super-LumiNova dial and has been kept in great condition for more than two decades. The case has been only lightly polished and remains very full. The original 93150 bracelet with CL-coded clasp has very mild stretch. The movement came to us in great shape, running at +3 s/d, with 269° amplitude and a 0.3 ms beat error. The watch comes complete with its original boxes, warranty papers and tag. It’s hard not to love a 14060: it’s slim and classy, yet still delivers everything a modern Submariner can. A superb example of a neo-vintage Rolex classic.

title: ROLEX SUBMARINER 14060 TRITINOVA DIAL
description: The Rolex Submariner 14060 was introduced in 1990, replacing the 5513, which had enjoyed a glorious 28-year production run. Although it looked similar to the white gold surround (WGS) 5513, the 14060 brought several key updates, including a sapphire crystal, the calibre 3000 movement and a unidirectional bezel. These significantly improved its functionality and robustness, while retaining the clean, symmetrical no-date look of the iconic Submariner. Over its production life, the 14060 went through several notable changes: from tritium to LumiNova dials and later, in 1999, to the 14060M (“modified”), which introduced a Super-LumiNova dial and the modern calibre 3130. This U-serial example is one of the anomalies the watch community has discovered over the years: a “Tritinova” dial. During a very narrow window in 1997–98, Rolex had already switched from tritium to LumiNova lume but continued to use up its existing dials printed with the tritium “T<25” marking. The case has been polished and shows the honest wear that came from being worn and enjoyed over the years. The dial carries the T<25 marking but glows brightly under UV, just like the later “Swiss” only LumiNova dials. The original U-stamped 93150 bracelet has only very mild stretch. The movement has been freshly serviced and is running perfectly at +2 s/d, with 275° amplitude and a 0.1 ms beat error. The watch comes with its original warranty, dated October 1998. A superbly cool neo-vintage Submariner, and a little snapshot of Rolex’s transitional years that will forever live in the past.

title: ROLEX EXPLORER II 16570 CHICCHI DI MAIS
description: Among Rolex’s offerings from what we now call the neo-vintage era, a “Chicchi” 16570 is easily one of my favourite configurations. It combines the everyday practicality of a five-digit Rolex, with features such as a sapphire crystal and an independently adjustable hour hand, with the unique charm of a creamy patina that develops over time, something more commonly associated with four-digit references. The 16570 was introduced towards the end of the 1980s, replacing the 16550, which had been in production for only a few years. Over time, collectors began to notice that the tritium lume on certain 16570s could age to a warm, creamy tone, earning these examples the nickname Chicchi di Mais (“corn kernels”). The present example dates to 1996 and is a great ambassador for the Chicchi. The tritium lume on the hour markers has aged to a rich, creamy hue, offering a beautiful contrast against the white dial. The lume on the hands is slightly lighter, which is extremely common on these watches. The case has been polished in the past but remains strong, and the original 78790/501B bracelet with Z-coded clasp has minimal stretch. The bezel shows some wear and partial loss of lacquer.

title: ROLEX SUBMARINER DATE 168000 'STARDUST' TRIPLE ZERO
description: The Submariner 168000 has always been a fun anomaly of the “transitional” era of the 1980s. In 1987, Rolex quietly released a watch that looked virtually identical to the Ref. 16800. Its only distinguishing feature was its 904L steel, which offered better corrosion resistance than the steel of its predecessor. After only nine months of production, Rolex introduced yet another new reference, the 16610, with an upgraded movement, and the 168000 disappeared as quietly as it had arrived. Rolex would not use another six-digit reference for more than twelve years, making the 168000 the first “six-digit Rolex” by a wide margin. The transitional Rolex models of the mid-1980s are some of my favourites. During this period, the brand reworked much of its line-up and experimented with new dial techniques and materials. Some of these were technically “imperfect”, yet resulted in wonderfully unique and beautiful characteristics, such as the “cream dial” 16550, the “tropical” 16760 and this, the “Stardust” 168000. It left the factory looking just like a 16800, but over the past four decades, the top lacquer on the dial has aged to create a mesmerising star-like pattern. The tritium lume on the markers and hands has aged to a gentle creamy hue. The case has been lightly polished in the past and retains thick lugs and strong crown guards. The original full-link 93150 bracelet has just been re-pinned by Michael Young and is now in as-new condition. The clasp is a 1999 Rolex service replacement. The movement has recently been serviced and is running superbly at +2 s/d, with 288° amplitude and a 0.1 ms beat error. Very, very cool.

title: ROLEX SUBMARINER 5513 GILT DIAL
description: When people talk about vintage Rolex, the 5513 is perhaps the first watch that comes to mind. It perfectly captures what we love about vintage watch collecting. Its production run of nearly three decades means the one reference includes many small variations, each with its own distinct look. Its robust construction means it is still perfectly good for everyday wear. And the magic of time has given each example its own character. I have always been fond of gilt-dial examples. In the galvanic process, the text and minute track were left as raised brass while the rest of the dial was treated to achieve a deep, glossy black finish. The result is a striking contrast that gives gilt dials their signature mirror-like appearance and incredible depth. This example dates from the later part of the brief 5513 gilt-dial era (circa 1962–1966). Production during these years was significantly lower than in the later matte-dial era, and gilt dials are estimated to account for only about 4% of all 5513s and 5512s made. The non-chapter-ring dial is stunning. All the plump tritium markers are intact and have aged beautifully, as have the hands, contrasting superbly with the glossy gilt dial, which is beginning to turn tropical around the edges. The lume glows brightly under UV and fades quickly afterwards. The original “Long 5” insert has aged to a beautiful lavender colour. The watch benefits from a recent (and very expensive) Rolex service. The case remains full despite the polish, and a new 93150 bracelet was fitted. It comes with the Rolex service box and NFC service card, which has another year of warranty left. A gorgeous 5513 that’s still amazing to wear.

title: ROLEX SEA DWELLER 1665 GREAT WHITE MK4 COLLECTOR SET
description: The Sea-Dweller was perhaps the only Rolex sports model created truly out of necessity: the state-of-the-art dive watch Rolex offered at the time, the Submariner, simply wasn’t up to the demands of a rapidly evolving subsea industry. Rolex initially modified the 5513 with a valve that allowed helium to escape from the case during decompression. This wasn’t entirely successful, so a completely new design with a new case was born. By 1971, Rolex had formed a partnership with COMEX, after Omega’s rocky relationship with the French diving company had come to an end. Rolex supplied COMEX with watches in return for detailed real-world testing and feedback. The Sea-Dweller Ref. 1665 was produced from 1967 to 1983, although it was only sold to civilians from around 1971. In the first years of production, the depth rating and “Sea-Dweller” text were printed in red, and these watches are affectionately known as “Double Red Sea-Dwellers”. From 1977 to 1983, five further dial variations appeared (Mk0 to Mk4), with the Sea-Dweller name and depth rating now printed in white, earning the nickname “Great White”. This 1981 example comes from the final years of 1665 production and has a Mk4 dial. It remains in fantastic condition after four decades. The case has been polished but remains full, with strong lugs and crown guards. The dial is perfect, with the tritium lume on the markers and hands aged to an even, creamy hue. The hands are free from oxidation, the original Mk3 insert has kept its colour, and the original silver date wheel is present. The full-link bracelet with F-stamped clasp is also original and in great shape. Amazingly, the original inner and outer boxes, tags, anchor, booklets, wallet, calendar, guarantee, translation papers and all the Rolex service paperwork have survived the test of time. The movement is running very healthily at +2 s/d, with 275° amplitude and a 0.2 ms beat error.

title: ROLEX SUBMARINER 6536-1 GOLD DEPTH TROPICAL DIAL
description: Early Submariners have always been some of the most collectible vintage watches from any brand. Between the relatively low production numbers (and far fewer surviving in original condition), the distinctive design that sets them apart from later models and, of course, the power of the brand, these watches tick every box in vintage watch collecting. The Ref. 6536/1 here is a great example. In a short production run of around four years, eight or nine variations left the Rolex factory, starting with the transitional 6536/8 with its red depth rating. The “gold depth” dial followed, as seen on this example. The original radium dial has thankfully survived the test of time and still gives a strong Geiger reading. The gilt lacquer has “gassed out”, leaving a wonderful tropical brown colour. The six o’clock marker is, correctly, slightly lighter than the rest, a deliberate (functional) design choice by Rolex. The 7206 fixed-rivet bracelet is a 1965 service replacement, and the insert is also a service replacement from the late ’60s. Despite turning 70 this year, the 37mm case remains very full and wears beautifully on the wrist. Small- and big-crown references are becoming increasingly difficult to find, with completely period-correct examples achieving six-figure prices. This is a beautiful and honest example of one of Rolex’s most compelling early Submariners. Do take up our offer on requesting additional images on this one.

title: FRANCK MULLER MAGNUM CHRONOGRAPH 6850 CC
description: If you were into watches in the 1990s and early 2000s, you’ll know that Franck Muller was one of the “hottest” brands on the market. It was particularly popular in Asia and often seen as a status symbol, thanks to its signature tonneau case and bold dial designs. Unfortunately, the brand’s popularity dropped significantly over the following two decades, perhaps because of the sheer number of models it introduced and heavy discounting, both in store and, in particular, on the secondary market. For us watch nerds, however, Franck Muller remains a formidable and, dare I say, rather nostalgic brand, especially in its early years. Founded in 1991 by Franck Muller and Vartan Sirmakes, the brand quickly gained a reputation for serious watchmaking. Muller himself was widely regarded as one of the finest watchmakers of his generation, having spent years restoring and studying some of the most complicated watches ever made. In the early days, the brand focused heavily on high complications, producing perpetual calendars, tourbillons and minute repeaters. Its first watches were traditional complications that, from a distance, many would mistake for Patek Philippe or Breguet. They were produced in extremely small numbers and remain among the most collectible examples of early independent watchmaking. Soon afterwards, Franck Muller developed the style it is now best known for: the tonneau-shaped Cintrée Curvex. The Magnum Chronographe Ref. 6850 CC here dates from the turn of the millennium and perfectly illustrates what Franck Muller is all about. Its 34 × 47mm 18k yellow gold case houses the Franck Muller calibre 2800CC. The dial has a three-register layout that is rather reserved by FM standards, complemented by the bold exploding numerals and a railway minute track. The watch has been freshly serviced and is running beautifully at +2 s/d, with 275° amplitude and a 0.3 ms beat error. A wonderful throwback to the glory days of FM.

title: LONGINES 7983-1 18K ROSE GOLD
description: Longines was founded in 1832 in Saint-Imier, Switzerland, and is one of the oldest watch brands still in continuous operation. In the early to mid-20th century, it was one of the leading manufacturers of precision timepieces, particularly known for its chronographs. These watches were also among the first to be catalogued, studied and collected when vintage watch collecting first emerged, helped in no small part by Longines’ remarkably detailed archive of serial numbers and production records spanning well over a century. Fast-forward to today, and vintage watch collecting is largely dominated by the likes of Rolex, Patek Philippe and Audemars Piguet. Longines, by comparison, is less frequently discussed, perhaps partly because of the brand’s modern positioning within the Swatch Group, where it sits below the top tier of Swiss watchmaking. As a result, there is a huge array of vintage Longines gems to be found at excellent value. The Ref. 7983-1 here dates from 1966 and has been kept in amazing shape. There are only minor marks on the silver dial, and the 34mm 18k rose gold case is in similarly fine condition. Inside, the calibre 370 was serviced within the last year and is running fantastically at −3 s/d, with 273° amplitude and a 0.6 ms beat error. At just under £2,500, this is a fantastic dress watch from one of Switzerland’s great powerhouses.

title: CHRONOFIXE TYPE 21 CHRONOGRAPH
description: In the early 1950s, the French Ministry of Defense required a purpose-built pilot’s watch for its Air Force and Naval Aviation, which led to the creation of the Type 20 and Type 21 chronographs. Much like the British Army’s W10, the Type 20 and 21 are military specifications rather than specific models. These watches were produced by several leading French manufacturers of the time, including Dodane, Airain, Auricoste, Vixa, and Mathey-Tissot. The most famous maker is undoubtedly Breguet, whose Type 20 remains a flagship model today—original examples often fetch tens of thousands. The present example is a Type 21 by Chronofixe, a military supplier/retailer whose watches were manufactured by Mathey-Tissot. And I must say, this is one of the most beautiful, balanced, and visually pleasing chronographs I've ever handled. The 38 mm case is unpolished, proudly showcasing its original bevels and sharp edges. The full radium dial and syringe hands are pristine, with all lume intact and now exhibiting a rich pumpkin patina. The two-register layout is clean, functional, and superbly legible. To complete the package, the watch retains its very rare “navigation” bezel. The watch was serviced in the last year, and it's running perfectly at +4 s/d, 320 amplitude, with a 0.4 ms beat error. Original Type 20s and 21s are incredibly hard to find, and this example is as good as any you’re likely to come across.

title: OMEGA SEAMASTER 300 CK2913-3
description: The Omega Seamaster 300 began its life in 1957 with the ref. CK2913, released alongside the Railmaster CK2914 and Speedmaster CK2915 to form the legendary “Master Trilogy.” While the Seamaster name dates back to the 1940s, the SM300 was Omega’s first true dive watch—built for serious underwater use and officially rated to 200 m (though tested to 300 m, hence the name). The CK2913 features a 38 mm straight-lug case, a thin bi-directional Bakelite bezel, and a clean, highly legible black dial. It remained in production for only a slender four years before being replaced by the CK14755. Much like the early no-crown-guard Rolex Submariners, Omega experimented with a wide range of design elements during this short period. The present watch, a CK2913-3, is the first example we’ve had in over a year—and what a watch it is. The original radium dial has beautifully tropicalised, giving it a rich and striking appearance. All radium markers are intact and glow brightly under UV. The “small broad arrow” hour hand and white lollipop seconds hand are both in fantastic condition. While the case has been lightly polished in the past, it remains full and sharp. Most impressively, the original Bakelite bezel insert is completely intact—an extremely rare occurrence on this reference. An Extract from the Archives confirms the watch was delivered to Gibraltar on 26 March 1958. Nearly 70 years later, it still holds all its charm and character. The movement has been freshly checked and is running perfectly at +3 s/d, with 293 amplitude and a beat error of just 0.1 ms. This is essentially Omega’s equivalent of the early Rolex “Big Crown” and “Small Crown” Submariners—but still at a comparatively attainable price point. It is absolutely gorgeous on the wrist. This OG SM300 is ready for its next chapter.

title: ZODIAC MONOPUSHER CHRONOGRAPH SECTOR DIAL FAB SUISSE VALJOUX 22
description: Founded in 1882 in Le Locle, Switzerland, by Ariste Calame under his eponymous brand, the name “Zodiac” was registered in 1908 and remains in use over a century later. Admittedly, Zodiac is not one of the most talked-about brands today, even among serious watch enthusiasts on forums and collector groups. Nevertheless, the company left behind an incredibly diverse catalogue of watches, most notably the Sea Wolf, widely regarded as one of the very first commercially available diving watches, alongside the Blancpain Fifty Fathoms and Rolex Submariner. The present example comes from the heyday of chronographs during the 1930s and 1940s, when they were increasingly used for professional and military applications. The design is unmistakably representative of the era, sharing many traits with contemporary models from manufacturers such as Rolex, Omega, Tissot, and Vetta. The 35.5 mm case was considered large for its time and wears beautifully on the wrist. Powering the watch is a Valjoux 22 monopusher movement. The star of the show, however, is the gorgeous sector dial, featuring a minute counter at 3 o’clock, running seconds at 9, a central chronograph seconds hand, and concentric telemeter, minute/seconds, hour, and tachymeter scales. These surround the Zodiac signature and the “Fab. Suisse” designation, indicating that the watch was originally imported and sold in France. The watch has survived in incredible condition nearly a century later. The sector dial is largely free from blemishes, while the fixed-lug case remains wonderfully sharp. We have freshly serviced the movement, which is running beautifully at +4 s/d, with 265° amplitude and a 0.4 ms beat error. Technicalities aside, this is one of the prettiest chronographs I've handled this year, ready for its next journey.

title: ETERNA 154FTP CHRONOGRAPH VALJOUX 72
description: As you can probably tell from our line-up, we’re big fans of ’60s and ’70s chronographs, and our love doesn’t stop at Rolex, Omega or Heuer. We’ve made it our mission to bring wonderfully made chronographs from other, somewhat forgotten brands, such as Certina, Glycine and Yema, to the world. Here we have the Eterna 154FTP chronograph. Eterna’s story began in 1856, when Josef Girard and Urs Schild founded Dr. Girard & Schild, a company that built its watches from the movement up. The Eterna name wouldn’t appear until 1906, and until the 1960s, the brand mainly produced small but robust time-only sports and dress watches. This watch, however, is Eterna’s answer to the ’60s sports chronograph renaissance. It may be something of an anomaly in Eterna’s history, but what a watch it is. The 39mm cushion case houses the legendary Valjoux 72, and unlike the more monochrome designs from Heuer or Rolex, Eterna painted a very different picture. The three white subdials are each decorated differently (even the fonts vary), set against a matte grey background that creates a striking “reverse panda” look. The dial is largely free from imperfections, and the lume has aged to a rich, dark pumpkin patina. The bezel insert is the star of the show: the “red wine” bezel has faded beautifully to a coppery hue, completing the watch perfectly. The caseback engraving reads 154FTP-3, with the “3” correctly denoting the dive bezel (the 154FTP-7, for example, has a tachymeter bezel). The case is in fantastic condition and has probably been polished no more than once or twice. It even comes on the very rare original Eterna bracelet, which has no stretch. Our watchmaker has inspected the movement, and it is running fantastically at +3 s/d, with 250° amplitude and a 0.3 ms beat error.

title: BREITLING NAVITIMER 806 AOPA MK 2.2
description: Among vintage chronograph enthusiasts, few would dispute that Breitling had as much of an impact as Heuer, Rolex or Omega, if not more, on the sports chronograph as we know it today. The brand’s most famous model is, of course, the Navitimer, originally developed in 1952 and still Breitling’s flagship today. The earliest Navitimers were produced exclusively for the Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association (AOPA). Powered by the renowned Valjoux 72 movement, they had an all-black dial signed with the AOPA logo. Produced for just one year, these so-called “pre-806” models are as rare as hen’s teeth and highly prized by collectors. In 1956, Breitling introduced the Ref. 806, now powered by the Venus 178 movement, a configuration that remained in use until the early 1970s. Many people associate the 806 with the familiar “reverse panda” dial and white subdials, but the earliest examples had all-black dials, and these are by far the most sought after among Breitling enthusiasts. The present watch is a very early (and rare) variation of the 806, with a Mk 2.2 dial. While many early Navitimers suffer from water ingress or movement issues, this nearly 70-year-old example has been preserved in astonishing condition. It is completely correct throughout, from the beaded bezel with its full 92 beads to the all-black dial with Breitling and Genève signatures, the stylised “B”, and the radium-lumed syringe hands and chronograph seconds hand. It is genuinely amazing on the wrist. This configuration, specifically the version without the “Genève” signature, was the reference point for Breitling’s 2019 “1959 Re-Edition”. The movement has had a full overhaul and is running at −1 s/d, with 310° amplitude and a 0.4 ms beat error. An original instruction manual accompanies the watch, which is perfect if you decide to use the circular slide rule to calculate fuel consumption on the M25.

title: ZENITH SUB SEA PILOT DIVER CHRONOGRAPH 01-0190-415
description: In January 1969, Zenith announced the El Primero, one of the world’s first automatic chronograph movements, and fitted it to some of the most gorgeous chronographs ever made, such as the A384 and A386. Despite the automatic movement, these watches are remarkably well proportioned and wear beautifully on the wrist. A few years later, Zenith put the same movement into a rather different watch: the Sub Sea Pilot/Diver, Ref. 01-0190-415. It has a 44mm tonneau case with a rotating bezel, offered with either a 12-hour aviation scale or a 60-minute diving scale. This is not a small watch on the wrist, and it was perhaps too large for the 1970s market too: it disappeared from Zenith’s catalogue after only a few short years. The timing could hardly have been worse. As the quartz crisis took hold, sales were slow, and in 1975 Zenith’s then American owners ordered mechanical production to stop and the tooling to be scrapped. It was only thanks to one employee, Charles Vermot, who secretly hid the El Primero plans and tools in an attic, that the movement survived to be revived in the 1980s. As a result, few examples of the 01-0190-415 have survived. Thankfully, this one has been preserved in amazing condition. The tritium lume has aged beautifully to a warm, creamy hue, and the case is in great shape, as is the bezel, save for a small crack at 10 o’clock. The lobster bracelet was made by Gay Frères in 1975. The movement is in excellent health and is running at +3 s/d, with 285° amplitude and a 0.5 ms beat error. Some 50 years later, the watch community has broadly concluded that a “diving chronograph” isn’t a very useful concept. Still, I’m glad watches like this exist. What fun.

title: OMEGA SEAMASTER 600 166.077 PLOPROF
description: In the late 1960s, the race to the depths was gathering pace. Offshore oil exploration, commercial saturation diving and military operations were pushing divers deeper and for longer than ever before, and Swiss watchmakers were racing in parallel to produce the most capable underwater tool. Omega’s answer was perhaps the most utilitarian watch ever made: the Seamaster 600 “Ploprof”, short for plongeur professionnel (professional diver). Developed in collaboration with COMEX, the Ploprof was unveiled at the 1969 Basel fair and went on general sale in 1971. The not-so-petite case has no removable caseback, the crown is secured by a screw-down locking nut, and the bezel can only be turned when the red button is pressed. An unwanted side effect of the sealed design, however, is that many Ploprofs suffer from dial degradation and bubbling, so original examples are rather hard to find. This example, with a non-C case, B1 bezel and D4 dial, has been preserved in fantastic condition, and under UV it is a sight to behold. The calibre 1002 is running beautifully at +3 s/d, with 295° amplitude and a 0.5 ms beat error. The mesh bracelet fits wrists of up to about 16cm, but Isofrane straps can be sourced on request. There’s nothing quite like a Ploprof.

title: OMEGA CONSTELLATION 168.5004 18K YELLOW GOLD DENNISON CASE
description: As a “professional” watch seller, my favourite part of the job, by far, is finding the most diverse and wonderful watches and presenting these amazing, sometimes overlooked, pieces to the world in all their glory. Selfishly, though, it’s just as enjoyable to admire and study them, and to imagine the days when they were first made. The Omega Constellation we have here is one of those time capsules we can’t help but love. The Constellation was introduced in 1948, originally as the limited-production Centenary Chronometer. It proved so popular that Omega decided to continue the concept, and in 1952 the Constellation as we know it today was formally born: a collection of automatic chronometers sitting at the very top of Omega’s range. Over the years, Omega produced the Constellation in countless variations, with different dial designs, bracelet constructions and case materials, ranging from stainless steel and gold plate to 9ct and 18ct gold. In mid-20th-century Britain, however, Omega faced a problem: high import duties on precious-metal watches made it uneconomical to import fully assembled gold cases. To solve this, Omega partnered with the British firm Dennison, which made cases domestically to Omega’s exacting standards. These proudly carried British hallmarks, “Made in England” signatures and the A.L.D. stamp for Aaron Lufkin Dennison. This particular watch is one of those Dennison-cased Constellations. Holding it today, you’d never guess it turns 63 this year. The 18ct yellow gold case is in fantastic condition, having seen very little polishing in its lifetime. The bracelet is a work of art in itself, made up of numerous individual links that drape beautifully around the wrist, and the clasp is every bit as delightful to use as it is to admire. The bracelet has been shortened in the past and will fit wrists of approximately 15–16cm. We will of course include a pair of leather straps from our friends at The Strap Tailor with the watch. The silver dial has aged gracefully, developing a subtle, darker patina in places. Onyx baton markers and the applied Constellation star complete the composition. The movement has been freshly serviced and is running at +5 s/d, with 286° amplitude and a 0.1 ms beat error. One can only imagine the life of the person who first bought this piece back in 1963. Today, it remains an unbelievably cool watch, available for little more than its melt value.

title: OMEGA SEAMASTER 14701SC 18K ROSE GOLD
description: The early Seamaster dress range is proof that tool watches don’t always have to look rugged. In the 1950s, it carried all the hallmarks of the early Seamaster line, being reliable, water-resistant and versatile enough for everyday wear, but dressed up in solid gold. At 34.5mm, the case has that sweet mid-century proportion: slim, refined and perfectly wearable today. The screw-down caseback ensured the watch lived up to the Seamaster’s reputation for durability, while inside ticked Omega’s calibre 501, a robust automatic movement with centre seconds. The “SC” in the reference stands for seconde centrale , highlighting that central-seconds feature. The watch is in excellent condition. The case has seen minimal polishing, the dial has developed a wonderful, even patina, and the alpha hands still retain their radium lume. The movement was serviced recently and is running at a commendable −2 s/d, with 285° amplitude and a 0.4 ms beat error. As solid 18k gold watches go, these are nearly unbeatable for value.

title: UNIVERSAL GENEVE POLEROUTER BUMPER 20217-4
description: For many vintage watch lovers, myself included, Universal Genève Polerouters hold a special place in our hearts. The elegant design, robust movements and sheer variety of references make the Polerouter one of the best watches to collect. It also helps that, for years, these watches were easy to find and very affordable (sadly, those glorious days are behind us…). In the 1950s, commercial aviation was rewriting the map. Scandinavian Airlines System (SAS) pioneered a bold new route over the North Pole, connecting Copenhagen and Los Angeles faster than ever before. To mark the occasion, SAS turned to Universal Genève to create a watch worthy of this milestone in modern exploration. The result was designed by a young Gérald Genta, who would go on to create some of the most iconic watches in horological history. At just 23, he conceived the Polarouter, as it was initially named. It was issued to SAS pilots and crew and built to handle extremes with both precision and style. Its reputation soon spread beyond the cockpit, the watch was renamed the Polerouter, and the rest is history. History aside, a time-only Polerouter is simply gorgeous. This example is an early Ref. 20217, powered by the legendary calibre 138SS “bumper” movement (if you’ve never owned one, you’re in for a treat…). It turns 70 this year and has aged better than most of us ever could. The black dial with its silver rehaut is striking, and the original radium markers are intact, having matured to a rich pumpkin patina with some variation in colour. The case has been polished but remains strong. The numbers on the caseback have worn away over the years. The movement came to us running beautifully at +3 s/d, with 275° amplitude and a 1.2 ms beat error. Wearing a Polerouter has never failed to put a smile on my face, and I hope this one brings as much joy to its next owner as it has brought us.

title: UNIVERSAL GENEVE 10373-2 MICROTOR
description: If we’ve crossed paths in the last few years, you’ll probably have heard me say that Universal Genève is my favourite brand. From the early 20th century to the 1970s, UG gave us an amazing catalogue of watches across many categories. In recent years, UG has finally begun to receive the recognition it deserves, particularly for its Polerouters and its sports chronographs from the ’60s. These were largely handmade and powered by legendary movements such as the Valjoux 72. Models such as the Compax “Nina” and Tri-Compax “Eric Clapton” now easily fetch five-figure sums. Early Polerouters had “bumper” automatic movements, such as the calibre 138SS, which I absolutely love, partly because of the satisfying bump you feel as the rotor reaches the end of its travel. In the mid-1950s, however, Universal Genève patented a revolutionary micro-rotor movement, in which the winding rotor was integrated into the movement rather than mounted above it. This allowed the manufacture to produce some of the thinnest automatic movements of the era. Although these micro-rotor movements are best known from the Polerouter, they also powered UG’s dress watches, such as this Ref. 10373-2. Value is notoriously hard to pin down in vintage watch collecting, but you’d have to be rather harsh to question it here. More than 60 years on, the 34mm 18k yellow gold case remains in amazing condition, with only hairline marks, and the sunburst silver dial is largely free of imperfections. The movement came to us in great shape, running at +5 s/d, with 255° amplitude and a 0.5 ms beat error. Perhaps victims of UG’s vast catalogue, “niche” pieces like this are still incredibly underappreciated and undervalued. They look gorgeous on the wrist and are sure to put a smile on their next owner’s face.

title: PIAGET PROTOCOLE TANK 18K YELLOW GOLD FULL SET
description: Founded in 1874 by Georges-Édouard Piaget in the village of La Côte-aux-Fées, Switzerland, Piaget began as a small workshop dedicated to crafting high-precision movements. By the mid-20th century, under the leadership of the founder’s descendants, the brand had begun producing watches under its own name, evolving from movement supplier into fully fledged luxury manufacture. Piaget quickly became synonymous with ultra-thin watchmaking. The calibre 9P (1957) and 12P (1960) were, at the time, the thinnest hand-wound and automatic movements in the world. The brand also supplied movements and technical expertise to some of Switzerland’s most prestigious houses. Many Cartier watches from the 1970s, for instance, were powered by Piaget-based calibres. Like many others, Piaget suffered during the quartz crisis, and in the late 1970s and early 1980s it shifted its focus towards high-end quartz watches. In 1979, it took a bold approach to the integrated-bracelet quartz watch with the Polo, available as the Ref. 7661 C701 (round) and 7131 C701 (square). In contrast to the extrovert Polo, the Protocole “Tank” here, produced alongside it in the same era, was one of the few watches that kept Piaget’s traditional craft alive through those turbulent years. Measuring just 20 × 23mm, it is powered by Piaget’s in-house ultra-thin calibre 4P. Despite its petite size, the watch is anything but simple: both the dial and every side of the case except the back are finely decorated. The watch has clearly been admired rather than worn over the years. There are barely any signs of wear, and the hallmarks on the caseback are as sharp as new. Amazingly, the previous owner kept the original warranty document and velvet pouch. A remarkable time capsule from the 1980s.

title: PIAGET POLO 18K YELLOW GOLD 7131 C701
description: Founded in 1874 by Georges-Édouard Piaget in the village of La Côte-aux-Fées, Switzerland, Piaget began as a small workshop dedicated to crafting high-precision movements. By the mid-20th century, under the leadership of the founder’s descendants, the brand began producing watches under its own name, evolving from a movement supplier into a fully fledged luxury manufacture. Piaget quickly became synonymous with ultra-thin watchmaking. The Calibre 9P (1957) and 12P (1960) were, at the time, the thinnest mechanical and automatic movements in the world. The brand also supplied movements and technical expertise to some of Switzerland’s most prestigious houses—1970s Cartier watches, for instance, often featured Piaget-based calibres. Like many others, Piaget suffered during the Quartz Crisis and shifted its focus in the late 1970s and early 1980s toward high-end quartz watches. During the time when quartz movements were introduced to models like the Rolex Day-Date, Patek Phillipe Nautilus, and Audemars Piguet Royal Oak, Piaget took an even bolder approach. In 1979, the Polo was introduced: an all-gold watch powered by an ultra-thin quartz movement, available as ref. 7661 C701 (round) and 7131 C701 (square). The Polo was also the first Piaget to carry its own model name, a departure from the brand’s long-held philosophy that “Piaget” itself was the product. It was also, at the time, the most expensive time-only watch on the market (more than double the price of a Day-Date). Perhaps as a result, only a few thousand Polos were produced in the decade following its debut, and many were sadly melted down for their gold during periods when they fell out of favour with collectors. Which makes it all the more special when an early example such as this ref. 7131 C701 appears. The watch has an unapologetically bold personality. In square form, the Polo is the ultimate expression of the integrated-bracelet sports watch. The case—if one can even distinguish it—is seamlessly absorbed into the 18k gold bracelet, powered by the ultra-thin Calibre 7P. The bracelet itself is a work of art. This example has been exceptionally well preserved, with no stretch and full links. In recent years, Piaget Polos have finally begun to receive the recognition they deserve, aided in part by the brand’s reintroduction of the Polo 79—once again vying for the title of the most extravagant two-hand gold watch on the market. It had a full Piaget service 2 years ago. A remarkable time capsule from

title: IWC NOVECENTO PERPETUAL CALENDAR IW3546
description: There is little doubt in my mind that neo-vintage IWC complications are among the most beautiful, yet overlooked and undervalued, watches on the market today. From the mid-1980s to the early 2000s, IWC was one of the few Swiss manufactures producing perpetual calendar wristwatches. This was largely thanks to Kurt Klaus’s remarkable perpetual calendar system, which did away with the usual cluster of correctors and pushers (often operated with a cocktail stick, as many perpetual calendar owners will know). Instead, his ingenious module can be adjusted entirely via the crown. It automatically accounts for the varying lengths of the months and for leap years, needing virtually no manual intervention beyond keeping the watch running. Alongside round-cased references such as the IW3750 and IW3751, IWC also quietly produced the Novecento line (Italian for “twentieth century”), with square and rectangular cases heavily inspired by the Art Deco designs of the 1920s and 1930s. The Ref. IW3546 here replaced the IW3545 in the late 1990s, although the two are nearly identical in design. The IW3545 was powered by the automatic calibre 32062, based on Frédéric Piguet’s celebrated calibre 953, whereas the IW3546 used the JLC-based calibre 96061. Although it lacks a traditional round case, the watch is simply stunning on the wrist, wearing much like a Cartier Tank despite housing a perpetual calendar. We have freshly serviced the watch, and it is running beautifully at +3 s/d, with 271° amplitude and a 0.4 ms beat error. The original gold buckle is still present. And yes, it’s cheaper than a modern Datejust.

title: IWC MK XI 6B/346 ROYAL AIR FORCE ISSUED
description: The IWC Mark XI 6B/346 holds a special place among collectors of vintage military watches. Issued to the British military from the late 1940s, these 36mm pilot’s watches are not only virtually indestructible, but also superbly balanced and legible on the wrist. Most Mark XIs you’ll come across have a circled T on the dial, indicating tritium lume, but they were originally issued with radium dials. It wasn’t until the 1960s that these were replaced with less radioactive tritium dials. This example dates from the very beginning of Mark XI production in 1948 and is easily one of the best we have ever seen. The stainless steel fixed-lug case is untouched, and a soft-iron inner cage protects the hand-wound calibre 89 from magnetic fields. The dial has survived in amazing condition, with pumpkin-toned lume and no imperfections. After a full service, the watch is running beautifully at +2 s/d, with 280° amplitude and a 0.2 ms beat error, nearly 80 years after it was made. The Mark XI went on to inspire many later IWC pilot’s watches, and this is as fine an example as you’ll find.

title: LEMANIA CHRONOGRAPH MONOPUSHER 'MOA ISSUED'
description: From the mid-1940s until around 1970, Lemania was the exclusive supplier of mechanical chronographs to the British military. To meet the Ministry of Defence’s specifications, these were all monopusher chronographs, with the start, stop and reset functions controlled by a single button at 2 o’clock, which helped prevent the chronograph from being started accidentally. In 1969, the MoD published a new specification, DEF-STAN 66-4, which was amended the following year to allow two-pusher chronographs. From then on, military chronograph supply was dominated by four manufacturers, all using the Valjoux 7733 movement: Hamilton, CWC, Newmark and Precista. The Lemania 6BB/924-3306 here was issued to the Royal Air Force in 1965 and is easily one of the nicest examples out there. The tritium lume on the markers has aged to an intense pumpkin hue, and the case is largely free of marks. Following a recent service, the watch is running beautifully at +5 s/d, with 250° amplitude and a 0.1 ms beat error.

title: ROLEX OYSTER PERPETUAL 36 PINK EXPLORER DIAL 116034 FULL SET
description: As a lover of vintage watches, I must admit that one of my guilty pleasures in the modern Rolex range is the 36mm Oyster Perpetual. It is simple and slim, yet it comes in fun, playful designs of a kind Rolex has rarely offered over the years. The introduction of colourful dials in recent years really propelled the popularity of the OP line, but Rolex began experimenting quite a bit earlier. The Ref. 116034 here dates from 2017 and has a fluted bezel and a very cool “Explorer” dial, with Arabic numerals at 3, 6 and 9. Instead of the usual white, however, all the hour markers are pink. And no, this isn’t a custom dial: Rolex really did make it this way. Nearly a decade later, these have become something of a fan favourite. They are hard to find in this part of the world, having been more popular in Asia, and are incredibly fun to wear. This example recently came through Rolex’s Certified Pre-Owned (CPO) programme and is supplied with its original box, warranty card and Rolex CPO card. The movement is running perfectly at +1 s/d, with 280° amplitude and a 0.0 ms beat error.

title: ROLEX DAY-DATE 18039 18K WHITE GOLD
description: It’s no secret that I love vintage and neo-vintage Day-Dates. They are slim and classy, and they represent mind-boggling value compared with both vintage sports models and modern Day-Dates. The 180xx series was introduced in the late 1970s and represents the second generation of the Day-Date line-up. It was fitted with the updated calibre 3055 movement and was the first Day-Date to feature a quick-set date. This small but significant upgrade makes the watch much easier to set when it is worn only occasionally as part of a collection. The Ref. 18039 here dates from 1983 and has an 18k white gold case, which was produced in much smaller numbers than the yellow gold version. The watch has been enjoyed over the years but has amazingly survived in fantastic condition, with an unpolished case. The dial, hands, German-language day wheel and date wheel were replaced by Rolex during a service last year. The movement runs beautifully at +3 s/d, with 291° amplitude and a 0.1 ms beat error. The original guarantee papers and booklets are still present, as is the NFC Rolex service card.

title: CHOPARD L.U.C. QUATTRO 16/1903 FULL SET
description: In 2000, Chopard surprised the watch world with one of haute horlogerie’s most interesting movements in some time: the L.U.C Cal. 1.98, with four barrels and an impressive nine-day power reserve. Amazingly, the team led by Chopard co-president Karl-Friedrich Scheufele fitted all of this into a compact 38mm case (Ref. 16/1863) just 9.5mm thick. The 16/1863 received COSC certification as well as the Geneva Seal. In 2007, the brand updated the “Quattro” line with the 16/1903 series (Mk II), and again in 2011 with the 16/1926 series (Mk III), which had larger cases. This example is from the second generation and has a 38mm 18k white gold case. Compared with the first-generation 16/1863, the 16/1903 has a bolder dial design. A white guilloché centre is surrounded by a contrasting black ring carrying the Arabic hour numerals, with a date and small seconds subdial at 6 o’clock and the power reserve indicator at 12 o’clock. The watch has been preserved in amazing condition over the years, with barely any wear. It comes with all its original boxes, paperwork and accessories. Neo-vintage dress pieces are finally getting the attention they deserve. With the current-generation Quattro starting at over £37,000, this remains one of the most overlooked watches from a top Swiss manufacture.

title: ROLEX SEA-DWELLER 1665 GREAT WHITE MK1
description: The Sea-Dweller was perhaps the only Rolex sports model created truly out of necessity: the state-of-the-art dive watch Rolex offered at the time, the Submariner, simply wasn’t up to the demands of a rapidly evolving subsea industry. The Ref. 1665 was produced from 1967 to 1983, although it was only sold to civilians from around 1971. In the first years of production, the depth rating and “Sea-Dweller” text were printed in red, and these watches are affectionately known as “Double Red Sea-Dwellers”. From 1977 to 1983, five further dial variations appeared (Mk0 to Mk4), with the Sea-Dweller name and depth rating now printed in white, earning the nickname “Great White”. The present example has a Mk1 dial, which is seen from around the 5.1m to early 6m serial ranges. Although these ranges overlap with Mk2 and Mk3 examples, Mk1s are, based on our own observations, much rarer. Having spent its entire life on the Scottish coast, this watch remains in fantastic condition. The case has been polished, but probably no more than once or twice. The dial is perfect, with the lume on the markers and hands aged to an even, creamy hue. The original silver date wheel is present, and the insert has faded beautifully to a grey-lavender tone. The original 93150/580 bracelet with F-coded (1981) clasp retains all its links and shows minimal stretch. The movement was serviced this year and is running like a dream at 0 s/d, with 280° amplitude and a 0.2 ms beat error.

title: ROLEX SEA-DWELLER 16660 'TRIPLE SIX' MATTE DIAL
description: In the Rolex dive watch lineage of the past 70 years, the Sea-Dweller 16660 “Triple Six”, introduced in 1978, arguably represented the single biggest technological leap forward. Produced alongside its predecessor, the 1665, it offered a significantly improved water resistance of 1,220 metres. This came from a more robust case, an enlarged helium escape valve and, for the first time on a Rolex dive watch, a sapphire crystal. It set a new benchmark for professional dive watches, and nearly 50 years later, one could argue that these features are still the blueprint for the modern dive watch. In the early years of production, Rolex fitted the 16660 with matte “Pallettoni” dials. In 1983/84, glossy “Bicchierini” dials were introduced, and they remained in use until the end of production. Despite having the lowest production numbers of any Sea-Dweller reference, the 16660 exists in a remarkable variety of dial executions, even more so than other transitional Rolex models of the period. These dials were made by several manufacturers, including Beyeler, Stern and Lemrich. This 1983 example has a Pallettoni dial made by Beyeler. The tritium lume on the markers and hands has aged to a rich, dark cream patina that contrasts wonderfully with the matte black dial, which itself has taken on a subtle tropical hue. As you can see, the watch has been used exactly as intended. The bezel has faded attractively, and the tritium pearl has developed a lovely warm tan. The case has been polished in the past but remains full and even, with no pinholes. It is fitted to its original 93160/592 bracelet with a P11 (November 1991) clasp, which is likely a service replacement. The movement has been freshly serviced and is running beautifully at +4 s/d, with 290° amplitude and a 0.2 ms beat error. We also replaced all the gaskets, and the watch passed a 10-bar pressure test. Examples like this make me fall in love with vintage Rolex over and over again.

title: HEUER CALCULATOR 150.633
description: In 1969, Heuer, alongside Breitling, Hamilton-Büren and Dubois Dépraz, unveiled the Calibre 11, one of the world’s first automatic chronograph movements. Heuer was quick to build a whole family of utilitarian sports chronographs around it, from the Monaco and the Carrera to the cushion-cased Autavia. There were a few oddballs among them too, and the Calculator has become one of the fan favourites. Introduced in 1972, the Calculator was originally designed for engineers, pilots and anyone else who regularly needed to multiply, divide or convert figures. Its rotating outer bezel works against a fixed inner scale to form a circular slide rule, so calculations can be read directly from the watch. It’s not a small watch, but its reasonable lug-to-lug length makes it surprisingly wearable. The Calculator was offered in two main versions. The models with symmetrical subdials, such as the Ref. 110.633, used the Calibre 12, with a 30-minute and a 12-hour register. The Ref. 150.633 here was powered by the Calibre 15, a simplified version of the Chronomatic movement with a running seconds subdial at 10 o’clock and a 30-minute counter at 2. The present example has a beautiful blue dial, which has been kept in fantastic condition over the years. The orange accents have kept their original colour, and the tritium lume has aged to an even, creamy hue. Following a recent health check, the movement is running beautifully at +6 s/d, with 271° amplitude and a 0.4 ms beat error.

title: HEUER AUTAVIA 1163 JO SIFFERT MEISTER DOUBLE SIGNED
description: Heuer introduced the Autavia in 1962 with the Ref. 2446, and over the following two decades released more than 90 variants of what would become its flagship sports chronograph. Early Autavias had round screw-back cases and three-register dials, with compressor cases following shortly afterwards. A major shift came in 1969, when Heuer, alongside Breitling, Hamilton-Büren and Dubois Dépraz, developed the Calibre 11, one of the world’s first automatic chronograph movements. The automatic Autavias moved to a cushion-shaped case, which remained in use until the quartz crisis brought Heuer’s golden era to an end. Among them, the 1163 T “Jo Siffert” is easily one of the most desirable, with its white dial and beautiful blue accents. Jo Siffert famously wore one almost constantly until his fatal accident in 1971. This example has survived in amazing condition. The white dial has taken on a gentle creamy patina, complemented by the tritium lume on the markers and hands, which has aged to the same gorgeous creamy hue. The blue accents on the markers and chronograph seconds hand have retained their full colour, as have the black inserts on the polished markers and the hour and minute hands. The icing on the cake is that the watch was originally retailed by Meister, the Zurich retailer that is still in business today, and the dial proudly bears the Meister signature. Double-signed Meister Heuers are few and far between, and to my knowledge, this is the only one currently for sale. The movement is running beautifully at +3 s/d, with 281° amplitude and a 0.2 ms beat error. An amazing Heuer.

title: DOXA SUB 300T SYNCHRON
description: Originally founded in 1889 by Georges Ducommun in Le Locle, Doxa began as a traditional Swiss watchmaker. However, it was in the mid-twentieth century that the brand truly made its mark in the world of dive watches. Among dive watch enthusiasts, Doxa is widely recognised as a true innovator in purpose-built underwater tools. The tonneau-shaped SUB 300 and SUB 300T not only featured bold, forward-thinking designs but also introduced technical innovations such as the helium escape valve and the unidirectional bezel, features later adopted by industry giants such as Rolex and Omega. Like many other brands, Doxa was hit hard by the Quartz Crisis. The SUB 300T, introduced in 1968, was discontinued just a few years later in the mid-1970s, leaving relatively few original examples in circulation today. Thankfully, the brand has enjoyed a revival in recent years, with a series of well-received reissues that have reignited interest in these historically significant watches. The present example features the most recognisable iteration of the original SUB 300T, with its bright orange dial: a colour chosen following extensive underwater visibility testing. The case proudly carries the character it has earned over the years, while the tritium dial remains spotless. We have paired the watch with a period lobster-style bracelet, although it looks equally at home on a beads-of-rice bracelet or a NATO. The movement has been freshly serviced and is running at +4 s/d, with 290° amplitude and a 0.3 ms beat error. The watch has also passed a 5-bar pressure test. There are few vintage dive watches that combine historical importance, technical innovation, rarity, and outright awesomeness quite like the SUB 300T. Such a formidable watch.

title: UNIVERSAL GENÈVE POLEROUTER 'MICROTOR' 20368-1
description: For many vintage watch nerds such as myself, Universal Genève Polerouters hold a special place in our hearts. The elegant design, robust movements, and sheer variety of references within the line-up make the Polerouter one of the most rewarding watches to collect. It also helps that, for many years, these watches were readily available on the market and remarkably affordable (sadly, those glorious days are now behind us...). In the early 1950s, commercial aviation was rewriting the map. Scandinavian Airlines System (SAS) pioneered a bold new route, charting a course over the magnetic North Pole to connect Los Angeles and Copenhagen faster than ever before. To mark the occasion, SAS turned to Universal Genève to create a watch worthy of this milestone in modern exploration. The result was a design by a young Gérald Genta, who would later go on to create some of the most iconic watches in horological history. At just 24 years old, he conceived the Polarouter (as it was initially named), issued to SAS pilots and crew, and built to perform in extreme conditions with both precision and style. It wasn’t long before its reputation extended far beyond the cockpit. The watch was soon renamed Polerouter, and the rest is history. Early Polerouters featured "bumper" automatic movements (such as the calibre 138SS), which we absolutely love—partly because of the satisfying bump you feel as the rotor reaches the end of its travel. In the mid-1950s, however, Universal Genève filed patent no. 329805, describing a revolutionary micro-rotor movement in which the winding rotor was integrated into the movement rather than mounted above it. This allowed the manufacture to produce some of the thinnest automatic movements of the era, including the calibre 218-9 found in this lovely ref. 20368-1. All the technicalities aside, a crosshair-dial, time-only Polerouter is simply gorgeous. This example has survived in wonderful condition over the years. The black dial with its silver rehaut is striking; the original dauphine hands, applied UG logo, and all of the original lume remain intact. The case is especially full on this one, and the engravings on the caseback are still beautifully crisp. We've paired the watch with these period stainless steel bracelet. The movement came to us running beautifully at +5 s/d, with 265° amplitude and a 0.7 ms beat error. Putting a Polerouter on has never failed to put a smile on my face, and I hope this one brings as much joy to its next owner as it

title: FRANCK MULLER PERPETUAL CALENDAR 5850 QP FULL SET
description: If you were into watches in the 1990s and early 2000s, you’ll know that Franck Muller was one of the “hottest” brands on the market. It was particularly popular in Asia and often seen as a status symbol, thanks to its signature tonneau case and bold dial designs. Unfortunately, the brand’s popularity dropped significantly over the following two decades, perhaps because of the sheer number of models it introduced and heavy discounting, both in store and, in particular, on the secondary market. For us watch nerds, however, Franck Muller remains a formidable and highly respected brand, especially in its early years. Founded in 1991 by Franck Muller and Vartan Sirmakes, the brand quickly gained a reputation for serious watchmaking. Muller himself was widely regarded as one of the finest watchmakers of his generation, having spent years restoring and studying some of the most complicated watches ever made. In the early days, the brand focused heavily on high complications, producing perpetual calendars, tourbillons and minute repeaters. Its first watches were traditional complications that, from a distance, many would mistake for Patek Philippe or Breguet. They were produced in extremely small numbers and remain among the most collectible examples of early independent watchmaking. Soon afterwards, Franck Muller developed the style it is now best known for: the tonneau-shaped Cintrée Curvex. The perpetual calendar Ref. 5850 QP here dates from 1999 and perfectly illustrates what Franck Muller is all about. Its 32 × 38.5mm 18k yellow gold case houses the Franck Muller calibre 2800, which is based on the ETA 2892 but fitted with FM’s in-house perpetual calendar module. The date, moon phase, month and day/leap year subdials at 3, 6, 9 and 12 o’clock respectively are complemented by the bold exploding numerals. The watch has been freshly serviced and is running beautifully at −3 s/d, with 265° amplitude and a 0.6 ms beat error. Putting it on the wrist takes you straight back to Hong Kong at the turn of the millennium. What a time that was.

title: ENICAR SHERPA JET GRAPH 300 'MKIV'
description: In the 1960s and ’70s, numerous iconic chronographs emerged from historic manufacturers such as Rolex, Omega, Breitling, Universal Genève and Heuer. In the shadow of these big names, Enicar also produced a series of exceptional sports chronographs in the 1960s, which have gained a cult following among collectors. Enicar began as the Manufacture d’Horlogerie Ariste Racine in La Chaux-de-Fonds, Switzerland, in 1913, founded by husband-and-wife duo Ariste Racine and Emma Blatt. A year later, the pair renamed the company “Enicar”: Racine spelt backwards. Over the following decades, Enicar steadily grew in popularity thanks to its exceptional quality for the price. At the 44th Basel Watch Fair in 1960, Enicar released the “Sherpa Graph”, which proved to be one of the brand’s most successful models, partly thanks to its association with legendary F1 driver Jim Clark, who famously wore one. Between 1960 and 1970, Enicar introduced a series of sports chronographs known as the “Graphs”: the Sherpa Graph, Aqua Graph, Jet Graph and Super Graph. The present example is the fourth and final iteration of the Jet Graph. Designed for pilots and frequent travellers, the Jet Graph adds a GMT function to the chronograph. It is powered by the Valjoux 724, a modified version of the famed Valjoux 72 with an added 24-hour hand. The Mk IV was made for only about a year, in 1969. Enicar did things its own way: the “reverse panda” three-register dial is complemented by playful details, including the vibrant red-orange chronograph hand, the chequered GMT hand, the 24-hour bezel and the red bezel pointer ring. The dial and hands are in great condition, with all the lume intact. The compressor case, supplied by Ervin Piquerez SA (EPSA) and similar to that of the Heuer Autavia, is in equally excellent condition and appears unpolished. Fewer than 500 Enicar “Graphs” are believed to have survived, making them among the rarest sports chronographs of the 1960s. This watch has recently been serviced and is running perfectly at −5 s/d, with 320° amplitude and a 0.4 ms beat error. An outstanding watch.

title: ROLEX GMT-MASTER 1675 TYPE C WIDE SWISS GILT DIAL
description: The GMT-Master 1675 is easily one of the most exciting references in vintage Rolex collecting. Not only did it go through numerous variations during more than 20 years of production, but thanks to its colourful bezels and the different lacquers, paints and lume used, each example has developed a truly individual character over the decades, often beautiful in very different ways. This 1966 example has a Type C gilt dial and is simply wonderful. The galvanic dial is gorgeous, with all the lume aged to a uniform, creamy hue. The case has been lightly polished in the past, and the 7836/382 bracelet has only mild stretch. The original “Pepsi” bezel has faded heavily in the blue section but retained its full red hue in the red half. The watch turns 60 this month and comes with its original boxes, wallet, guarantee and chronometer papers. It was serviced last year and is running smoothly at +2 s/d, with 250° amplitude and a 0.1 ms beat error. There’s just nothing quite like a gilt 1675.

title: OMEGA JUMBO CHRONOGRAPH CAL. 33.3
description: In the world of Omega chronographs, the calibre 321 is by far the most famous movement, and deservedly so. It powered the CK2915, the very first Speedmaster, and since its recent revival it has once again become the flagship movement of the current Speedmaster range. However, its lesser-known ancestor, the cal. 33.3, is arguably more collectible and most certainly rarer. Based on a Lemania design and shared with Tissot within the SSIH group, the calibre 33.3 was introduced in the early 1930s and remained in production for around two decades. Despite that long run, fewer than 14,000 are believed to have been made. These movements powered a range of Omega chronographs, from snap-back models such as this one to water-resistant references such as the CK2077, original examples of which now fetch astronomical sums. The 33.3 is widely recognised as the predecessor of the cal. 321. Historical importance aside, it is also one of the most beautiful chronograph movements ever made. When this watch came through the door, I couldn’t wait to pop open the caseback and admire the incredibly well-kept cal. 33.3. The watch itself has also survived in outstanding condition, and its 37.5mm case is extremely large for the period. The white multi-scale dial has an outer tachymeter, a telemeter scale for calculating distance using the speed of sound, and an inner decimal ring. It is finished with gorgeous leaf hands and a chronograph seconds hand with a beautiful spade-shaped tail. The dial has a gentle creamy patina, and the printing has been lightly retouched in the past, as is the case with many examples from this period. More than 80 years on, the watch still runs remarkably well at +8 s/d, with 255° amplitude and a 1.2 ms beat error. It was made in Switzerland while the world was in the depths of the Second World War. Simply incredible.

title: AUDEMARS PIGUET CAL.2612 GREY DIAL
description: The Royal Oak is undoubtedly one of the most iconic watches of all time. It arguably saved Audemars Piguet, and Gérald Genta’s legendary 1972 design has shaped the brand ever since. Yet the manufacture produced an incredible range of watches both before and after the Royal Oak’s debut. Fast-forward to today, and the Royal Oak continues to dominate the brand’s image and demand. As a result, some fantastic 20th-century APs with exceptional craftsmanship fly under the radar and still offer remarkable value. The present example dates from the 1980s and is a wonderful product of its time. The 1970s and 80s were an incredibly difficult period for the Swiss watchmaking industry. Quartz made the mechanical movement all but obsolete in practical terms, almost overnight. Even the biggest brands scrambled to “adapt” to the new technology, and some didn’t survive long enough to try. Thankfully, AP just about made it through, and a few decades later, quartz APs from this era are fascinating to study and collect. This example has a 31mm 18k white gold stepped case with a beautiful grey dial. Mercifully, the two-hand design means we don’t have to witness a second hand ticking on a quartz watch. The watch was rarely worn and is unpolished, and the hallmarks on the caseback are as sharp as on day one. The original leather strap and 18k buckle are both present. A new battery has been fitted. A gorgeous AP that looks amazing on any wrist.

title: ROLEX DATEJUST 36 16014 TAPESTRY DIAL
description: It’s hard to beat a neo-vintage Datejust, especially one with a cool dial. The Rolex Datejust 160xx series was arguably the last generation with a truly vintage look: an acrylic crystal, drilled lugs, a slim case and, of course, a tritium dial. The Ref. 16014 here has a white gold bezel and a beautiful silver tapestry dial. These are easily among the most attractive Datejusts. The textured surface plays wonderfully with the light, and as an added Easter egg, the dials often age to cream or sometimes salmon. This one has an off-white hue. The watch came to us in amazing condition, with a minimally polished case and a spotless dial, with all the creamy tritium lume intact. The original 62510H bracelet with I-stamped clasp shows virtually no stretch. We have just serviced the watch, and it is running nicely at +3 s/d, with 265° amplitude and a 0.3 ms beat error.

title: ROLEX DAY-DATE 18038 'BLUE DIAL' COLLECTOR SET
description: Despite the overwhelming popularity of sports watches, the Day-Date has always been Rolex’s flagship and top-of-the-range model. Introduced in the 1950s, its iconic design has barely changed in the seven decades since. The 180xx series represents the second main generation of the Day-Date line-up. It brought the updated calibre 3055 movement and was the first Day-Date with a quick-set date. (If you’ve ever owned a four-digit Day-Date, you’ll appreciate how much of a difference this makes…) This 1985 example is easily one of the most beautiful 18038s you’ll ever see. Its sunburst blue dial plays wonderfully with the light and offers a striking contrast to the 18k yellow gold case. The original bracelet shows minimal stretch after more than four decades, and the previously polished case remains strong. All the lume plots are intact, and the day and date wheels have taken on a lovely matching patina. There is minor oxidation on the hour markers. The watch comes with its original inner and outer boxes, leather notebook, wallet, calendar, tags, handkerchief, original guarantee papers and all the service papers. The movement is running beautifully at +2 s/d, with 281° amplitude and a 0 beat error. An absolutely stunning Day-Date that we are proud to present.

title: ROLEX EXPLORER II 16550 WGS CREAM DIAL
description: As far as “transitional” Rolex references go, the Explorer II 16550 is among the most interesting and desirable. Following the lukewarm commercial reception of the Ref. 1655 “Steve McQueen” (hard to imagine today), the 16550 was introduced with a new movement offering a quick-set date, hacking seconds and the novel addition of an independently adjustable GMT hand. Despite its short four-year production run, the 16550 went through several dial variations. Early examples had white gold surrounds (WGS) on the hour markers, while later ones switched to black surrounds. By far the most desirable are the so-called “cream dial” versions. Owing to a manufacturing imperfection, the dials of certain 16550s aged to a striking creamy tone, most commonly on WGS examples. This example dates from the very beginning of 16550 production, in 1984, and time has blessed it with a lovely creamy dial. The gentle off-white hue is complemented by the cream-toned tritium markers in their white gold surrounds and the tritium hands. The watch has been kept in amazing condition over the years. The case has been polished, but only lightly, and the original wide-font bezel is in equally good shape. The 78360/501B bracelet is a 2006 service replacement. The movement has been freshly serviced and is running beautifully at +3 s/d, with 271° amplitude and a 0.0 ms beat error. Cream-dial 16550s have become some of the most collectible vintage Rolex watches in recent years, and this is a fantastic example to enjoy every day.

title: AUDEMARS PIGUET 15048BA 18K YELLOW GOLD
description: We’ve waited years, but smaller dress watches are finally making a comeback. Since the introduction of the Royal Oak in 1972, Audemars Piguet’s identity has been inextricably linked with it. Half a century later, the Royal Oak’s popularity has only continued to rise, while many of AP’s dressier offerings from the 1990s and early 2000s have fallen into relative obscurity. Whether this is simply a result of the sports watch boom of the past decade is open to debate, but the unexpected outcome is that some truly wonderful watches from this era can still be bought at remarkably reasonable prices. The Ref. 15048 here has a 32 mm 18k yellow gold case and a matching gold dial. Thanks to its thin bezel, however, it wears more like a 34 mm and looks wonderful on the wrist. This example has clearly been admired rather than worn over the years. There’s barely any wear visible, even on the original leather strap and 18k yellow gold buckle. The watch has been freshly serviced and is running perfectly at +2 s/d, with 251° amplitude and a 0.2 ms beat error. It comes with its original warranty papers and booklets. A prime example of how a beautiful precious-metal watch from a Holy Trinity brand needn’t cost tens of thousands of pounds.
